[00:32:59] **Sofia Bergström:** Exactly that. The template exists so nobody starts from nothing, but the ones that actually get responses have your voice in them, not ours. Doing it faster than that tends to mean you have not actually learned anything from the first wave before starting the second.

[00:33:18] **Mats Rehn:** So realistically we are looking at all twelve being contacted across five or six months if we do three waves of four.

[00:33:27] **Sofia Bergström:** That is a realistic estimate, yes, and it is worth saying that a five or six month timeline for genuinely engaging twelve suppliers properly is actually fast compared to most accounts I have seen, many of whom are still on their first wave a year in because nobody structured the sequencing at all. Structure alone, without any additional cleverness, is most of what separates a fast campaign from a slow one. Most of the accounts that struggle are not lacking cleverness, they are lacking a plan.

[00:34:02] **Mats Rehn:** That matches what our own experience with supplier programmes has generally been. I will structure it that way.

[00:34:10] **Sofia Bergström:** Do you have a sense of which two or three you would start with? I ask because the choice matters more than people expect.

[00:34:19] **Mats Rehn:** Probably our largest dairy supplier and one of the two big oil suppliers, both relationships I would describe as genuinely warm, people I could call directly rather than going through a formal channel.

[00:34:33] **Sofia Bergström:** That is exactly the right instinct. Starting with a relationship where somebody will pick up the phone rather than route you to a general inbox is the single biggest predictor of whether a first campaign gets a usable result inside three months.

[00:34:50] **Mats Rehn:** Is there a version of this that goes badly? I would rather hear the failure mode now than discover it myself in month two.

[00:35:00] **Sofia Bergström:** The version that goes badly is when a company starts with a cold relationship because it happens to be their biggest supplier by volume, gets silence or a slow bureaucratic response, and loses momentum before the warmer relationships ever get approached. Size of the relationship should never be the reason you go first, warmth should.

[00:35:23] **Mats Rehn:** That is a useful distinction and it is not one I would have made on my own, I would have defaulted to biggest supplier first because that is how procurement usually thinks about priority.

[00:35:37] **Sofia Bergström:** It is a completely reasonable instinct in most of procurement, it just does not transfer well to this specific kind of request, because you are not negotiating a contract, you are asking somebody to do you a favour that benefits them less directly than it benefits you.

[00:35:56] **Mats Rehn:** Good, that confirms what I was already leaning toward.

[00:36:00] **Sofia Bergström:** Good. And Mats, one honest flag before you commit your team's time. Some suppliers will simply say no, or go quiet. It is not a reflection on how the ask is made, some relationships are just not there yet.

[00:36:15] **Mats Rehn:** What is a realistic response rate, roughly, for the first wave? I want to set expectations properly with my own team before we start.

[00:36:25] **Sofia Bergström:** For a warm relationship approached properly, somewhere between sixty and eighty percent respond with something usable, in my experience.

[00:36:33] **Mats Rehn:** And what does something usable actually mean in practice? A perfect answer, or something rougher than that?

[00:36:40] **Sofia Bergström:** Rougher, in most cases, at least initially. I do not want to set an unrealistic bar for a first ask. Usable means they gave you real numbers rather than a database average, even if those numbers come with caveats or gaps you will need to work through. The perfect answer is rare in a first response and is usually something you build toward over two or three cycles of the relationship, not something you get on the first ask. Treating the first response as the final answer is a mistake I see accounts make repeatedly.

[00:37:19] **Mats Rehn:** That is a more realistic bar than I was picturing, and honestly a more achievable one for my team to aim at. It drops considerably for a colder relationship, sometimes below twenty percent, which is exactly why starting with your warmest two or three matters as much as it does. A cold response rate under twenty percent can genuinely demoralise a team before they have learned anything useful from the attempt, which is its own cost beyond the missed data. I have watched a team lose interest in an initiative entirely after one badly sequenced first wave.

[00:37:59] **Mats Rehn:** So the sequencing is not just about getting an early win, it is genuinely about the response rate itself.

[00:38:07] **Sofia Bergström:** It is both. A strong early response rate also becomes evidence you can use with the colder suppliers later, along the lines of, twenty of your peers have already done this. That single sentence does more work than almost anything else in a follow up request.

[00:38:25] **Mats Rehn:** Does that actually work, citing peer participation, or is it the kind of thing that sounds good in theory and does nothing in practice?

[00:38:35] **Sofia Bergström:** It genuinely works, and I have seen it demonstrated directly, an account of ours ran a proactive supplier offer with that exact framing on a second wave and it moved the response rate meaningfully compared to their first, colder attempt. [00:39:01] **Mats Rehn:** Good to know, I will make sure whoever drafts our second wave email includes that line specifically.

[00:39:14] **Sofia Bergström:** Most people would rather know, and almost nobody asks, so I appreciate you asking directly rather than finding out the hard way.

**Deal notes added by Sofia Bergström 2026-09-02:**

Nordflor signed. Forty two thousand, twelve month term. Closed in fifty one minutes with almost no friction on price, which after four months of security and legal, I did not expect.

Lars Torell, their CFO, asked for twelve months instead of twenty four and did not negotiate price at all. His reasoning: ordinary capital discipline plus a bad prior experience with a two year software contract that went unused for sixteen months after the first eight. I gave him twelve without a fight, per what we agreed after the last two closes. A resentful twenty four month customer is worth less than a happy twelve month one who renews.

I asked for one thing in return, not commercial: if they do not renew, I want the real reason in real time rather than a note that says budget eight months after the fact. He agreed easily, which is either a good sign or means nothing at all, I genuinely cannot tell which yet.

Ylva raised something worth recording. The security and legal process, four rounds of redlines, a security questionnaire, all of it, made the deal feel more real to her rather than less, and it is apparently what kept it alive internally when nothing above her was pushing urgently. That contradicts what I would have assumed, that the back half of a deal drains energy. For Nordflor it built commitment instead.

Before Lars joined, Ylva asked me directly whether the reduction planning gap gets better in a year. I did not promise her anything. I gave her the narrow honest answer instead, that measurement alone produces real decisions sometimes, Rapsverket being the example, and that it is not the same thing as the pathway Göran has asked about twice. She said she would rather have the narrow honest answer than a wide one that turns out to be soft, which is close to word for word what Mette Krogh at Aalborg told Karin in the exit interview. I did not know about that call when I said it. Worth noting how often the same instinct shows up on both sides of this.

Mats Rehn confirmed the ranking screen reframed four hundred and thirty one suppliers into a manageable list of twelve covering sixty eight percent of the footprint, and that this alone is what unlocked his side of the deal. He is sequencing in waves starting with the strongest relationships, on my advice.

Onboarding to Petra. This is our fourth close of the quarter and our biggest since Tre Kronor.
